To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the most difficult video databases are the ones that contain videos recorded in the wild and (2) the most challenging videos are those where the signing hand frequently crosses the face and/or other body parts.

the most challenging sign language recognition databases for tracking are the ASL database, the Bielefeld Sign Language Database, the Sign Language Recognition Project, and the Sign Language Recognition and Translation Database.

(1) the use of the blue-boxing environment for the tracking of the head and hands in sign language recognition is not necessary, and that (2) the use of a single video database for benchmarking tracking algorithms in sign language recognition scenarios is not sufficient.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of a tracking framework for video-based sign language recognition.

the following three aspects: (i) the development of a benchmarking framework for the evaluation of tracking algorithms in the context of sign language recognition, (ii) the analysis of tracking algorithms w.r.t. their tracking performance, (iii) the analysis of the impact of tracking errors on the performance of sign language recognizers.
the development of robust tracking algorithms for sign language recognition and with the development of a benchmark database for tracking algorithms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no database can be recommended for the evaluation of head and hand trackers for sign language processing, as the existing databases are too small and the annotations are too coarse.
the performance of tracking algorithms is highly dependent on the database used for the evaluation.
there is no video database available that is suitable for tracking benchmarking in a sign language recognition scenario.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there exist no public video databases that can serve as a common benchmark for video-based sign language recognition systems.
the tracking of the signing hand is a very challenging task, and that the use of special devices such as gloves is still required to obtain accurate tracking results.
the tracking performance of the state-of-the-art algorithms is far from being satisfactory.
The main takeaway from our work is that

tracking error rates can be used to evaluate and compare tracking algorithms, but the tracking error rates are usually not sufficient to evaluate the performance of sign language recognition algorithms.
there is a clear need for video-based sign language databases that contain ground-truth labels for head and hand tracking.
there is a lack of publicly available databases that are suitable to evaluate tracking algorithms in the context of continuous sign language recognition.
